questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a Hydrilla bubble-count experiment with Blackman's law of limiting factors (light, CO2 and temperature)
questions.question: A twig of Hydrilla in tap water at 20 °C is lit by a lamp of increasing intensity, and the oxygen bubbles released per minute are counted. Results: at intensities 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 (arbitrary units) the counts are 10, 20, 30, 31 and 31. At intensity 5, adding a pinch of sodium bicarbonate raises the count to 52. At intensity 1, warming the water to 30 °C leaves the count at 10. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) At low intensities light is the limiting factor, so the rate rises in proportion to light; above intensity 3 the rate levels off because another factor, CO₂, has become limiting, which is why bicarbonate (a CO₂ source) raises it; warming has no effect at intensity 1 because light, not temperature, is the factor in shortest supply there — as Blackman's law states, the rate is set by the factor nearest its minimal value
B) Light becomes harmful above intensity 3, and bicarbonate protects the chloroplasts from damage
C) Temperature is the main limiting factor at all light intensities, so warming should have raised the count at intensity 1
D) The levelling off shows that all the chlorophyll has been destroyed, and bicarbonate makes new chlorophyll
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Light limits at low intensity, CO₂ limits at high intensity, and temperature cannot act while light is limiting.
Concept: Photosynthesis is affected by several external factors (light, CO₂ concentration, temperature, water) and internal ones. Blackman's (1905) law of limiting factors states that if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest its minimal value; it is the factor that directly affects the process if its quantity is changed. Light saturation occurs at about 10 % of full sunlight, and above that other factors become limiting. CO₂ is the major limiting factor in nature because its concentration in air is very low (about 0.03–0.04 %).
Why: Between intensities 1 and 3 each step of light raises the count by the same amount, so light is limiting. From 3 to 5 the count barely changes: light is no longer limiting, and supplying extra CO₂ (bicarbonate) raises the rate sharply, showing that CO₂ was now the limiting factor. The dark (biosynthetic) reactions are enzyme-controlled and temperature-sensitive, but at intensity 1 the supply of ATP and NADPH from the light reaction is too low, so warming cannot speed things up.
Why not the others: (B) The rate did not fall, so there is no sign of damage, and bicarbonate is a carbon source, not a protectant. (C) The unchanged count at 30 °C shows temperature was not limiting at low light. (D) Destroyed chlorophyll could not respond to bicarbonate by increasing the rate.
Key point: Only the factor in shortest supply controls the rate; raising any other factor has no effect until that one is relieved.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Absolute versus relative growth rate of two leaves, and the arithmetic and geometric growth equations
questions.question: In one week, leaf P grows from 4 cm² to 8 cm² and leaf Q from 40 cm² to 44 cm². Which statement about their growth, and about the types of growth in plants, is correct?
options: A) Both have the same relative growth rate because both added 4 cm²
B) Q has the higher relative growth rate because it is larger; arithmetic growth is described by \(W_1=W_0e^{rt}\)

C) Both show the same absolute growth (4 cm² per week), but the relative growth rate of P is 100 % per week and that of Q only 10 % per week; in arithmetic growth only one daughter cell keeps dividing and length rises linearly (\(L_t=L_0+rt\)), whereas in geometric growth both progeny cells keep dividing, giving exponential growth (\(W_1=W_0e^{rt}\)) that slows into a sigmoid curve as nutrients become limited
D) P has a higher absolute growth rate; geometric growth gives a straight line when size is plotted against time
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Equal absolute growth, relative growth rate 100 % (P) and 10 % (Q); linear arithmetic and exponential geometric growth.
Concept: Growth can be measured as absolute growth rate (growth per unit time) or relative growth rate (growth per unit time per unit initial size). In arithmetic growth, after mitotic division only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures, as in an elongating root at constant rate; a plot of length against time is a straight line. In geometric growth, both progeny cells retain the ability to divide; growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase), and finally slows to a stationary phase as nutrients become limited, giving a sigmoid curve.
Given: P: 4 → 8 cm²; Q: 40 → 44 cm² in one week.
Formula/Principle: Absolute growth = final size − initial size; relative growth rate = absolute growth ÷ initial size.
Step 1: Absolute growth: P = 8 − 4 = 4 cm²; Q = 44 − 40 = 4 cm².
Step 2: Relative growth rate: P = 4/4 = 1 = 100 % per week; Q = 4/40 = 0.1 = 10 % per week.
Why: The two leaves add the same area, but P adds an area equal to its own original size, so its efficiency of growth is ten times that of Q. Relative growth rate is the better measure for comparing systems of different sizes.
Why not the others: (A) Equal absolute growth does not mean equal relative growth. (B) Q's relative rate is lower, and \(W_1=W_0e^{rt}\) describes geometric (exponential) growth. (D) The absolute growths are equal, and the straight line belongs to arithmetic growth.
Key point: Relative growth rate = absolute growth ÷ initial size; arithmetic growth is linear, geometric growth is exponential and then sigmoid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the events of normal inspiration, from muscle contraction to air flow, and the role of muscles in expiration
questions.question:
The following events occur during normal inspiration in humans:
P. The intra-pulmonary pressure falls below the atmospheric pressure.
Q. The diaphragm contracts, and the external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribs and sternum.
R. Air moves from outside into the lungs.
S. The volume of the thoracic chamber increases in the antero-posterior and dorso-ventral axes.
T. The pulmonary volume increases.
Which sequence is correct, and which statement about expiration is also correct?
options: A) P → Q → S → T → R; expiration always needs contraction of the abdominal muscles

B) Q → S → T → P → R; normal expiration occurs when the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, returning the thoracic and pulmonary volumes to normal so that intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric and air is expelled, while additional abdominal muscles help only in forceful breathing
C) Q → T → S → R → P; expiration occurs when the diaphragm contracts more strongly
D) S → Q → P → T → R; during expiration the intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Q → S → T → P → R; normal expiration is passive, driven by relaxation of the inspiratory muscles.
Concept: Breathing works by creating a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere. Inspiration happens when intra-pulmonary pressure is lower than atmospheric pressure (negative pressure in the lungs relative to air), and expiration when it is higher. The diaphragm and a specialised set of muscles, the external and internal intercostals between the ribs, help to generate these gradients.
Why: Muscle contraction comes first (Q). Contraction of the diaphragm increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis, and the lifting of ribs and sternum increases it in the dorso-ventral axis (S). Because the lungs follow the chest wall, the pulmonary volume rises (T), so the intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric (P), and air rushes in (R). Relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostals reverses these changes, and air leaves. With the help of additional muscles in the abdomen we can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.
Why not the others: (A) The pressure falls only after the volume rises, and quiet expiration does not need the abdominal muscles. (C) Pulmonary volume rises after the thoracic volume, the pressure fall comes before air flow, and expiration involves relaxation. (D) Muscle contraction must come first, and during expiration the pressure rises above atmospheric.
Key point: Muscles contract → chest volume up → lung volume up → pressure down → air in; relaxation reverses it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing lymph with blood plasma and distinguishing hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina and heart failure
questions.question: Which comparison of lymph and of disorders of the circulatory system is entirely correct?
options: A) Lymph contains red blood cells and all plasma proteins; angina is the stopping of the heart beat
B) Hypertension is a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg; in heart failure the heart muscle is suddenly killed by lack of blood
C) Lymph is formed only in the lacteals; coronary artery disease is caused by a weakened heart valve

D) Lymph (tissue fluid) has the same mineral distribution as plasma but lacks red blood cells and the larger proteins, and it carries absorbed fats from the lacteals; hypertension is blood pressure at or above 140/90 mm Hg; coronary artery disease is narrowing of the arteries supplying the heart muscle by deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue; angina is acute chest pain when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle; and heart failure is the heart not pumping blood effectively enough, with congestion of the lungs as a main symptom
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) All the statements about lymph, hypertension, CAD, angina and heart failure are correct.
Concept: As blood passes through capillaries, some water and small water-soluble substances move out into the spaces between cells, forming interstitial fluid or tissue fluid; larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the vessels. This fluid is collected by lymphatic vessels and drained back into the major veins, so lymph is a specialised connective tissue fluid. Lymph contains specialised lymphocytes responsible for immune responses, and fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals of the intestinal villi.
Why: Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg; repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart diseases and also affects vital organs such as the brain and kidneys. Coronary artery disease (often called atherosclerosis) narrows the lumen of the coronary arteries. Angina (angina pectoris) can occur in men and women of any age, more commonly in the middle-aged and elderly, when blood flow to the heart muscle is reduced. Heart failure is different from cardiac arrest (the heart stops beating) and heart attack (heart muscle is suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply).
Why not the others: (A) Lymph lacks RBCs and larger proteins, and angina is chest pain, not cardiac arrest. (B) 120/80 is normal, and sudden muscle damage describes a heart attack. (C) Lymph forms from tissue fluid in all tissues, and CAD is narrowing of the coronary arteries, not a valve defect.
Key point: Lymph = plasma minus large proteins and RBCs; hypertension ≥ 140/90; CAD = narrowed coronary arteries; angina = chest pain; heart failure = ineffective pumping.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating daily filtrate and the percentage reabsorbed from GFR and urine volume, and the steps of haemodialysis in uremia
questions.question: A healthy adult has a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 125 mL min⁻¹ and produces 1.5 L of urine per day. What volume of filtrate is formed per day, what percentage of it is reabsorbed, and which description of haemodialysis for a patient with kidney failure is correct?
options: A) 7.5 L per day; 80 % reabsorbed; in dialysis blood is passed through a fluid containing more urea than plasma

B) 180 L per day; about 99 % reabsorbed; blood drawn from a convenient artery is mixed with an anticoagulant (heparin), pumped through coiled cellophane tubes bathed in a dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except for nitrogenous wastes, so the wastes diffuse out, and the cleared blood is returned through a vein after adding anti-heparin
C) 180 L per day; 50 % reabsorbed; the dialysing fluid contains no salts, so that all ions are removed from the blood
D) 1.8 L per day; 17 % reabsorbed; heparin is added after the blood is returned to the body to stop clotting inside the vein
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 180 L per day; about 99 % reabsorbed; haemodialysis removes urea by diffusion into a plasma-like fluid without wastes.
Concept: The amount of filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute is the glomerular filtration rate; in a healthy individual it is about 125 mL per minute, i.e., 180 litres per day. Since urine released is only about 1.5 litres a day, nearly 99 % of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules. In kidney malfunction, urea accumulates in the blood (uremia), which is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure; urea can be removed by haemodialysis using an artificial kidney.
Given: GFR = 125 mL min⁻¹; urine = 1.5 L per day.
Formula/Principle: Filtrate per day = GFR × minutes per day; % reabsorbed = (filtrate − urine) ÷ filtrate × 100.
Step 1: Minutes per day = 24 × 60 = 1440; filtrate = 125 × 1440 = 180 000 mL = 180 L.
Step 2: Reabsorbed = 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 L; percentage = 178.5 ÷ 180 × 100 ≈ 99.2 %.
Why: The dialysing fluid has no nitrogenous wastes, so a concentration gradient drives urea and other wastes out of the blood across the porous cellophane, while useful ions at plasma levels are not lost. Heparin prevents clotting in the machine, and anti-heparin restores normal clotting before the blood goes back into the body.
Why not the others: (A) 7.5 L is the hourly filtrate, and a fluid with more urea would drive urea into the blood. (C) Only 1.5 L of 180 L leaves as urine, and salt-free fluid would strip useful ions from the blood. (D) 1.8 L confuses units, and heparin is added before, not after, the machine.
Key point: GFR 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day, about 99 % reabsorbed; dialysis fluid = plasma minus wastes, with heparin and then anti-heparin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using response speed, transcription inhibitors and receptor location to tell membrane-receptor hormones from intracellular-receptor hormones
questions.question: Two hormones, X and Y, act on the same target cells. X acts within seconds, raises the level of cyclic AMP in the cell, does not enter the cell, and still acts when a drug that blocks transcription is present. Y acts only after some hours, its receptor is found inside the cell, and its effect is abolished by the transcription-blocking drug. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) X is a steroid that regulates genes; Y is a peptide that acts through cAMP
B) Both act through intracellular receptors, so their actions differ only in speed
C) X must be a hormone that is not carried in the blood

D) X binds a membrane-bound receptor and acts through a second messenger (such as cAMP, IP₃ or Ca²⁺) that changes cell metabolism, as protein hormones such as FSH do; Y, like steroid hormones and iodothyronines, binds an intracellular receptor, and the hormone–receptor complex interacts with the genome to alter gene expression, which is why it needs transcription and acts slowly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) X uses a membrane receptor and second messenger; Y uses an intracellular receptor and changes gene expression.
Concept: Hormones produce their effects by binding to specific proteins called hormone receptors located in the target tissues only. Receptors present on the cell membrane are membrane-bound receptors, and those inside the cell are intracellular receptors, mostly nuclear receptors. Binding forms a hormone–receptor complex, which leads to biochemical changes in the target tissue. Hormones that interact with membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the target cell; they generate second messengers (e.g., cyclic AMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) which in turn regulate cellular metabolism. Hormones that interact with intracellular receptors (e.g., steroid hormones, iodothyronines) mostly regulate gene expression or chromosome function.
Why: A response within seconds that raises cAMP and survives a transcription block must work by modifying existing enzymes through a second messenger, so X uses a membrane receptor. Y needs transcription, its receptor is internal, and its slow response fits a change in the set of proteins being made, as with steroid hormones.
Why not the others: (A) The properties are reversed. (B) X does not enter the cell and acts without new transcription, so its receptor is on the membrane. (C) Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood; nothing in the data suggests otherwise.
Key point: Membrane receptor → second messenger → fast metabolic change; intracellular receptor → gene expression → slow change.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Working out chromosome numbers of embryo, perisperm, seed coat, pericarp and synergid from the endosperm number, with examples of seed types
questions.question: In a flowering plant, each endosperm cell has 36 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in a cell of (i) the embryo, (ii) the perisperm, (iii) the seed coat, (iv) the pericarp and (v) a synergid of the embryo sac? Which accompanying statement is also correct?
options: A) 24, 24, 24, 24, 12; perisperm is residual persistent nucellus found in seeds such as black pepper and beet, and the tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm
B) 24, 36, 12, 24, 12; the perisperm is formed by fertilisation of the polar nuclei
C) 36, 24, 24, 36, 24; the seed coat develops from the ovary wall
D) 12, 24, 36, 24, 12; the embryo is triploid because it receives two male gametes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 24, 24, 24, 24, 12; perisperm in black pepper and beet; coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm.
Concept: Double fertilisation gives a diploid zygote (egg + one male gamete) that becomes the embryo, and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (two polar nuclei + the other male gamete) that becomes the endosperm. The integuments of the ovule harden into the seed coat and the ovary wall develops into the pericarp, both maternal (2n) tissues. Remnants of the nucellus may persist in some seeds as perisperm (black pepper, beet). The synergids are haploid cells of the embryo sac, formed by mitosis from the haploid functional megaspore.
Given: endosperm = 3n = 36.
Formula/Principle: n = 36 ÷ 3; embryo, nucellus/perisperm, integuments/seed coat and ovary wall/pericarp = 2n; synergid = n.
Step 1: n = 12, so 2n = 24.
Step 2: Embryo 24, perisperm 24, seed coat 24, pericarp 24, synergid 12.
Why: Only the endosperm is triploid; every tissue derived directly from the mother plant (nucellus, integuments, ovary wall) carries the sporophyte number 2n, the embryo is 2n from fertilisation, and the embryo sac cells are n. In coconut, the endosperm begins as free nuclei (the water), which later become cellular (the white kernel).
Why not the others: (B) Perisperm is nucellus, not a fertilisation product, so it is 2n, and the seed coat is 2n. (C) The embryo is 2n, the pericarp is 2n, the synergid is n, and the seed coat comes from the integuments. (D) The embryo is diploid from one male gamete, and the seed coat is 2n.
Key point: Endosperm 3n; embryo, perisperm, seed coat and pericarp 2n; embryo-sac cells n.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the hormones of pregnancy, the placenta's roles, the signals of parturition and the value of colostrum
questions.question: Which comparison of events in pregnancy, birth and lactation is correct?
options: A) hCG, hPL and relaxin are made only by the pituitary gland; the levels of estrogens and progestogens fall during pregnancy
B) Parturition begins when the mother's hypothalamus decides that pregnancy is complete, independently of the foetus; colostrum contains no antibodies

C) The placenta, formed by finger-like chorionic villi interdigitating with the uterine tissue, supplies oxygen and nutrients, removes CO₂ and wastes, and acts as an endocrine tissue producing hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestins; relaxin is also secreted by the ovary in later pregnancy; parturition is induced by a neuroendocrine mechanism in which signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta cause mild uterine contractions (the foetal ejection reflex), triggering release of oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions; the yellowish milk of the first few days (colostrum) contains several antibodies (IgA) that protect the newborn
D) The foetus and mother share the same blood through the umbilical cord; oxytocin decreases uterine contractions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The placenta is a nutritive, excretory and endocrine organ; foetal signals start the foetal ejection reflex and oxytocin release; colostrum carries IgA.
Concept: After implantation, chorionic villi and uterine tissue become interdigitated and jointly form the structural and functional unit between the developing embryo and the maternal body, the placenta, connected to the embryo by the umbilical cord. During pregnancy, the levels of other hormones such as estrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine are increased several fold in maternal blood; these are essential for foetal growth and maintenance of pregnancy. The average duration of human pregnancy is about 9 months (gestation).
Why: Vigorous contraction of the uterus at the end of pregnancy expels the foetus (parturition); the signals originate from the fully developed foetus and placenta, which induce mild uterine contractions, and these cause oxytocin release from the maternal pituitary, which acts on the uterine muscle to cause stronger contractions, and so on (a positive feedback). The mammary glands produce milk towards the end of pregnancy, and the first milk, colostrum, provides passive immunity.
Why not the others: (A) hCG, hPL and estrogens/progestins come from the placenta, and these hormones rise during pregnancy. (B) The foetus and placenta start the signal, and colostrum is rich in antibodies. (D) Maternal and foetal blood do not mix, exchange occurs across the placenta, and oxytocin strengthens contractions.
Key point: Placenta = exchange + endocrine organ (hCG, hPL); foetal ejection reflex → oxytocin → stronger contractions; colostrum = IgA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Deducing autosomal recessive inheritance from a described two-generation pedigree and calculating carrier and offspring probabilities
questions.question: In a family, both parents (I-1 and I-2) are unaffected. Of their three children, II-1 (a daughter) is affected, while II-2 (a son) and II-3 (a daughter) are unaffected. II-2 marries an affected woman. What is the mode of inheritance, what is the probability that II-2 is a carrier, and what is the probability that the first child of II-2 and his wife is affected?
options: A) Autosomal recessive; 2/3; 1/3
B) X-linked recessive; 1/2; 1/4
C) Autosomal dominant; 1; 1/2
D) Autosomal recessive; 1/2; 1/4
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Autosomal recessive; II-2 is a carrier with probability 2/3; first child affected with probability 1/3.
Concept: Pedigree analysis traces a trait through several generations of a family. An affected child of two unaffected parents shows that the trait is recessive and that both parents are carriers. An X-linked recessive trait is expressed in a daughter only if her father is affected, since she receives his only X chromosome.
Given: unaffected parents; affected daughter; II-2 unaffected; his wife affected (aa).
Formula/Principle: Aa × Aa → 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; among unaffected children, P(Aa) = 2/(1 + 2).
Step 1: Unaffected parents with an affected child ⇒ recessive; affected daughter with an unaffected father ⇒ not X-linked; so autosomal recessive and both parents are Aa.
Step 2: II-2 is unaffected, so he is AA or Aa in the ratio 1 : 2 ⇒ P(carrier) = 2/3.
Step 3: Aa × aa gives aa with probability 1/2 ⇒ P(child affected) = 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3.
Why: Once we know II-2 is unaffected, the aa class is excluded, leaving AA and Aa in the ratio 1 : 2. The wife is aa and always passes a; the child is affected only if II-2 is a carrier and passes a.
Why not the others: (B) The affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive. (C) Two unaffected parents cannot have an affected child for a dominant trait. (D) Uses 1/2 instead of 2/3 for the carrier probability and then forgets the wife always passes a.
Key point: Unaffected sibling of an affected child (both parents Aa) is a carrier with probability 2/3.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing offspring of two colour-blindness crosses, and why haemophilic females and colour-blind females are rare
questions.question: Cross 1: a colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. Cross 2: a woman who is a carrier for colour blindness marries a man with normal vision. Which comparison is correct?
options: A) In cross 1 all sons are colour-blind; in cross 2 all daughters are colour-blind
B) Both crosses give half of the sons and half of the daughters colour-blind
C) In cross 1 half of the daughters are colour-blind; haemophilic females are common because the gene is dominant

D) In cross 1 none of the children is colour-blind, but all daughters are carriers and all sons are normal; in cross 2 about half of the sons are colour-blind and half of the daughters are carriers, but no daughter is colour-blind; colour blindness affects about 8 % of males but only about 0.4 % of females, and a haemophilic female arises only when the mother is at least a carrier and the father is haemophilic, which is extremely rare
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cross 1: carrier daughters, normal sons; cross 2: half the sons affected, half the daughters carriers.
Concept: Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in certain genes on the X chromosome; it results in defects in the red or green cones of the eye. A son of a carrier woman has a 50 % chance of being colour-blind. Haemophilia is also sex-linked recessive: a single protein in the cascade involved in blood clotting is affected, so a simple cut may cause non-stop bleeding. A heterozygous female (carrier) may transmit the disease to her sons.
Why: Cross 1: XᶜY × XX → daughters XᶜX (carriers), sons XY (normal), because a father gives his X only to daughters. Cross 2: XᶜX × XY → sons XᶜY or XY (1 : 1), daughters XᶜX or XX (1 : 1), all with normal vision, since each daughter gets a normal X from her father. A colour-blind or haemophilic daughter needs a mutant X from each parent; in haemophilia such females are very rare also because the disorder is often fatal in the later stages of life.
Why not the others: (A) Sons of cross 1 receive the mother's normal X; daughters of cross 2 receive the father's normal X. (B) No daughter is affected in either cross. (C) The gene is recessive, and haemophilic females are rare.
Key point: X-linked recessive: an affected father makes all daughters carriers; a carrier mother affects half her sons.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing lac-operon expression in the wild type and in i-gene, non-inducible repressor and lacZ mutants, with and without lactose
questions.question:
E. coli strains are grown with lactose (and no glucose) and without lactose. Which comparison of their lac-operon products is correct?
Strain 1: wild type.
Strain 2: the i gene is deleted.
Strain 3: the repressor still binds the operator but can no longer bind the inducer.
Strain 4: the z gene has a mutation that inactivates its product.
options: A) Strain 2 makes no enzymes at all; strain 3 makes all three enzymes only when lactose is present
B) Strain 4 cannot make permease or transacetylase, because the three genes form one operon

C) Strain 1 makes β-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase only with lactose; strain 2 makes all three whether or not lactose is present, because no repressor is formed; strain 3 makes none of them even with lactose, because the repressor stays on the operator; strain 4 makes permease and transacetylase only with lactose but no active β-galactosidase, so it cannot split lactose into glucose and galactose
D) All four strains behave identically, because lactose alone controls the operon
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Inducible (1), constitutive (2), non-inducible (3), and inducible without active β-galactosidase (4).
Concept: The lac operon has a regulatory gene i (coding for the repressor) and three structural genes: z codes for β-galactosidase, which hydrolyses the disaccharide lactose into the monomers galactose and glucose; y codes for permease, which increases the permeability of the cell to β-galactosides; and a codes for transacetylase. Lactose is the substrate and also the inducer. In the absence of inducer, the repressor binds the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon. In the presence of inducer, the repressor is inactivated by interaction with the inducer, and transcription proceeds. This regulation by lactose is negative regulation.
Why: Strain 2 has no repressor, so the operator is never blocked and transcription is constitutive. In strain 3, the inducer cannot inactivate the repressor, so the operator stays blocked even with lactose (a non-inducible strain). Strain 4 is transcribed normally when induced, but the mutant z product is inactive; y and a are separate genes on the same mRNA and their products are normal.
Why not the others: (A) Strain 2 is constitutive, not silent, and strain 3 cannot be induced. (B) A mutation that inactivates the z product does not destroy the y and a products. (D) The repressor and its interactions decide the response, so the strains differ.
Key point: No repressor → always on; repressor that cannot bind inducer → always off; inducer works by inactivating the repressor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering fossil-bearing rock layers by age and classifying pairs of organs as homologous or analogous
questions.question: In an undisturbed series of sedimentary rocks, layer W (the topmost) contains fossil horses, layer X below it contains dinosaur fossils, layer Y below X contains early amphibians, and layer Z (the deepest) contains jawless fish. Which age order (oldest first) and which classification of organ pairs is correct?
options: A) W → X → Y → Z; the wings of a butterfly and of a bird are homologous

B) Z → Y → X → W; the forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetahs and humans are homologous (divergent evolution), the thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are homologous, while the eye of an octopus and that of a mammal, and the flipper of a penguin and that of a dolphin, are analogous (convergent evolution)
C) Z → X → Y → W; the sweet potato and the potato are homologous because both store food
D) Y → Z → W → X; homologous organs always perform the same function
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Z → Y → X → W; forelimbs and thorn/tendril are homologous, eyes and flippers are analogous.
Concept: Fossils are remains of hard parts of life forms found in rocks. Rocks form sediments, and a cross-section of the earth's crust indicates the arrangement of sediments one over the other during the long history of the earth; different-aged rock sediments contain different life forms, which probably died during the formation of that sediment. Comparative anatomy also gives evidence: homologous organs have the same structure and origin but may perform different functions (divergent evolution), while analogous organs perform similar functions but are not anatomically similar (convergent evolution).
Why: In undisturbed rocks the deepest layer is the oldest, so Z (jawless fish) is oldest, followed by Y (amphibians), X (dinosaurs) and W (horses), which matches the known sequence of vertebrate evolution. The forelimbs share the same bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges), and the thorn and tendril both arise from axillary positions, so both pairs are homologous. The octopus and mammalian eyes, and the penguin and dolphin flippers, look and work alike but evolved independently, so they are analogous.
Why not the others: (A) Topmost is youngest, and butterfly and bird wings are analogous. (C) Amphibians appear before dinosaurs, and sweet potato (a root) and potato (a stem) are analogous. (D) The order is wrong, and homologous organs often have different functions.
Key point: Deeper rock = older fossils; same origin = homologous (divergent); same function only = analogous (convergent).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining antibiotic resistance with Darwin's natural selection, and distinguishing it from Lamarckian and mutation-on-demand explanations
questions.question: When a new antibiotic is used widely, after some years most infections are caused by resistant bacteria. Which explanation follows Darwin's theory of natural selection?
options: A) The antibiotic forced each bacterium to change its body during its lifetime, and these acquired changes were inherited, as with the long neck of the giraffe
B) The antibiotic directly caused the needed resistance mutations in bacteria that were in contact with it
C) Large single-step mutations created a new species of bacterium overnight, which is the main idea of Darwin's theory

D) Heritable variation already existed: a few bacteria were resistant before the antibiotic was used; in its presence they survived and reproduced more, leaving more offspring (greater reproductive fitness), so over generations resistant forms came to dominate, just as dark moths increased in industrial England — evolution by natural selection acting on pre-existing variation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Selection favours resistant variants that already existed, which then leave more offspring.
Concept: Darwin, based on observations during the voyage of HMS Beagle, concluded that existing living forms share similarities with one another and with forms that existed millions of years ago. Two key concepts of his theory are branching descent and natural selection. Populations have built-in variation in characteristics; those characteristics that enable some to survive better in natural conditions will outbreed others. Fitness, according to Darwin, ultimately refers to reproductive fitness: those who are better fit in an environment leave more progeny. He was also influenced by Malthus's ideas on populations: populations could grow exponentially, yet their size remains fairly constant, so there must be a struggle for existence.
Why: In nature the antibiotic acts as a selecting agent, killing sensitive bacteria. Resistant variants, which arose earlier by chance, leave more descendants, and the frequency of resistance rises. Similarly, excessive use of herbicides, pesticides and drugs selects resistant varieties in a much shorter time scale; these are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action.
Why not the others: (A) This is Lamarck's theory of use and disuse with inheritance of acquired characters. (B) The environment selects; it does not create the needed mutations. (C) Saltation (single-step large mutation) was Hugo de Vries' idea, not Darwin's gradual selection.
Key point: Natural selection acts on existing heritable variation; fitness means leaving more offspring.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: How memory cells explain primary and secondary responses, antibody structure, and active versus passive immunity
questions.question: A child receives a vaccine against a disease. Months later, the child is exposed to the real pathogen and shows no illness. Which explanation of the mechanism is correct?
options: A) The vaccine (inactivated or weakened pathogen, or its antigenic proteins) caused a primary response in which B and T lymphocytes produced memory cells; on exposure, these memory cells mounted a rapid and highly intensified secondary (anamnestic) response, with B cells producing antibodies, each made of four peptide chains (two light and two heavy, H₂L₂); this is active immunity, whereas giving ready-made antibodies, as in colostrum (IgA) or anti-tetanus or anti-venom injections, gives quick but passive immunity
B) The vaccine contained ready-made antibodies that stayed in the blood for life, so this is passive immunity
C) The vaccine made the child's skin impermeable to all microbes, which is an innate barrier
D) Antibodies are made by T lymphocytes, and each antibody is a single peptide chain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Memory cells from the primary response give a fast, strong secondary response; vaccination is active immunity, ready-made antibodies give passive immunity.
Concept: Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and is characterised by memory. The first encounter with a pathogen produces a primary response of low intensity; a later encounter with the same pathogen produces a highly intensified secondary (anamnestic) response, because the body remembers the first encounter. Primary and secondary immune responses are carried out by two special types of lymphocytes: B-lymphocytes, which produce antibodies (humoral immune response), and T-lymphocytes, which help B cells produce them and mediate cell-mediated immunity.
Why: Vaccination introduces a preparation of antigenic proteins of the pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen; the antibodies produced neutralise the pathogenic agents during actual infection, and the vaccines also generate memory B and T cells that recognise the pathogen quickly on subsequent exposure. When the host's own body makes antibodies in response to an antigen, it is active immunity. When ready-made antibodies are given directly to protect the body, it is passive immunity, used when a quick immune response is needed, as in tetanus or snakebite.
Why not the others: (B) Vaccines contain antigens, not antibodies, and the immunity is active. (C) Vaccination works through the immune system, not by changing skin permeability. (D) B-lymphocytes produce antibodies, and an antibody has four chains.
Key point: Vaccine → memory cells → fast secondary response (active immunity); injected antibodies = passive immunity; antibody = H₂L₂.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the number and direction of DNA bands in agarose gel electrophoresis after cutting circular and linear DNA, and how bands are seen
questions.question: A circular plasmid and a linear DNA molecule each contain two sites for EcoRI. After complete digestion, the fragments are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis. How many fragments does each give, and which statement about the gel is correct?
options: A) 3 fragments from the plasmid and 2 from the linear DNA; DNA moves towards the cathode because it is positively charged

B) 2 fragments from the plasmid and 3 from the linear DNA; DNA moves towards the anode because it is negatively charged; smaller fragments move farther through the agarose matrix (a natural polymer from sea weeds), and the bands are seen as bright orange under UV light after staining with ethidium bromide, then cut out and eluted for use
C) 2 fragments from each; larger fragments move farther than smaller ones
D) 4 fragments from the plasmid and 3 from the linear DNA; bands are seen in ordinary light without any stain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 and 3 fragments; DNA moves to the anode, small fragments farthest, seen orange under UV with ethidium bromide.
Concept: The cutting of DNA by restriction endonucleases results in fragments of DNA, which are separated by gel electrophoresis. Since DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules, they can be separated by forcing them to move towards the anode under an electric field through a medium/matrix; the commonly used matrix is agarose, a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds. The fragments separate according to their size through the sieving effect of the agarose gel: the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves. Separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation, as bright orange bands; the bands are cut out from the gel and extracted (elution).
Given: two EcoRI sites in each molecule.
Formula/Principle: Number of fragments: circular DNA = number of cuts; linear DNA = number of cuts + 1.
Step 1: Plasmid: 2 cuts in a closed ring → 2 fragments.
Step 2: Linear DNA: 2 cuts in a line → 3 fragments.
Why: Cutting a ring once only opens it; each further cut adds one piece. A linear molecule already has two ends, so the first cut already produces two pieces.
Why not the others: (A) Counts are reversed and DNA is negatively charged. (C) Linear DNA gives 3 pieces, and small fragments move faster. (D) Overcounts, and DNA bands are invisible without staining.
Key point: Circular DNA: fragments = cuts; linear: cuts + 1; DNA runs to the anode, small fragments farthest.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the ideas of biosafety approval, biopiracy and patents to the basmati case and similar Indian examples
questions.question: An Indian research group wants to release a genetically modified crop for farmers, and an Indian newspaper reports that a foreign firm has patented a rice variety derived from Indian basmati. Which statement about these situations is correct?
options: A) In India, a GM crop can be released by its developer without any approval, and biopiracy refers to stealing GM seeds from a laboratory
B) The basmati patent was granted to the Indian Government in 1997, and biopiracy is legal under all national laws

C) The Indian Government has set up the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC), which decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services; biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, without compensatory payment; in 1997 an American company got patent rights on basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office, for a variety derived from Indian farmers' varieties, and similar attempts have been made to patent uses of turmeric and neem, so India amended its patent laws to protect such resources
D) Patents cannot be granted for any product derived from living organisms anywhere in the world
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) GEAC approves GM work and releases; biopiracy is unauthorised, uncompensated use of bio-resources, as in the basmati case.
Concept: Genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem, so the Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC to make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services. Certain companies have been granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region or country.
Why: India has 27 documented varieties of basmati, valued for its unique flavour and aroma; the patented new variety had been derived from Indian farmer varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention. Industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, whereas developing nations are rich in biodiversity, which creates the possibility of exploitation. The Indian Parliament has cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, which takes such issues into consideration.
Why not the others: (A) GM organisms need GEAC approval, and biopiracy refers to exploiting traditional bio-resources. (B) The patent went to an American company, and biopiracy is what laws try to prevent. (D) Patents on biological products and technologies have been granted, which is exactly the issue.
Key point: GEAC regulates GM organisms in India; biopiracy = unauthorised, uncompensated use of bio-resources (basmati, turmeric, neem).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating logistic growth rates at a quarter, half and three-quarters of the carrying capacity and finding where growth is fastest
questions.question: A population follows logistic growth with intrinsic rate of natural increase r = 0.4 per year and carrying capacity K = 1000. What is the growth rate dN/dt (individuals per year) when N = 250, 500 and 750?
options: A) 100, 200, 300 — growth keeps increasing with N
B) 75, 100, 75 — growth is fastest at N = K/2 and is equal at N = K/4 and N = 3K/4
C) 75, 50, 25 — growth is fastest at the smallest population
D) 0, 100, 0 — growth occurs only at N = K/2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 75, 100 and 75 individuals per year; growth is fastest at K/2.
Concept: No population can grow exponentially for ever, since resources become limited. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows an initial lag phase, followed by acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote, when the population density reaches the carrying capacity (K), the maximum number the habitat can support. The plot of N against time is a sigmoid curve, called Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth, described by dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K.
Given: r = 0.4 yr⁻¹; K = 1000; N = 250, 500, 750.
Formula/Principle: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K.
Step 1: N = 250: 0.4 × 250 × 750/1000 = 0.4 × 250 × 0.75 = 75.
Step 2: N = 500: 0.4 × 500 × 0.5 = 100.
Step 3: N = 750: 0.4 × 750 × 0.25 = 75.
Why: The term N rises as the population grows, while the factor (K − N)/K, the environmental resistance, falls; their product is greatest when N = K/2 and symmetric about it. Since resources are finite, the logistic model is considered more realistic than exponential growth.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the (K − N)/K factor. (C) At small N there are few breeders, so growth is not fastest there. (D) Growth is positive at all N between 0 and K.
Key point: Logistic growth: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, maximum at N = K/2 and zero at N = K.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the discoveries about viruses and viroids chronologically and describing lichens as pollution indicators
questions.question:
Arrange these events in chronological order, and choose the correct accompanying statement.
P. Stanley showed that viruses could be crystallised and that the crystals consist largely of proteins.
Q. Ivanowsky found that the agent of mosaic disease of tobacco could pass through bacteria-proof filters, so it was smaller than bacteria.
R. Diener discovered a new infectious agent, smaller than viruses, that caused potato spindle tuber disease.
S. Beijerinck showed that the extract of infected tobacco plants could cause infection in healthy plants and called the fluid "contagium vivum fluidum".
options: A) P → Q → S → R; viroids have a protein coat but no nucleic acid
B) Q → P → R → S; lichens grow well in heavily polluted areas
C) S → Q → R → P; viruses can reproduce outside living cells

D) Q → S → P → R; viroids are free RNA without a protein coat, of lower molecular weight than viral RNA; and lichens, symbiotic associations of algae (phycobionts) and fungi (mycobionts), do not grow in polluted areas, so they are good pollution indicators
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ivanowsky (1892) → Beijerinck (1898) → Stanley (1935) → Diener (1971); viroids are naked RNA; lichens indicate clean air.
Concept: Viruses were not considered truly living, since they are inert outside the living cell; once they infect a cell they take over its machinery to replicate themselves, killing the host. Ivanowsky (1892) recognised certain microbes as the causal organisms of mosaic disease of tobacco; Beijerinck (1898) demonstrated the infectious fluid; Stanley (1935) showed viruses could be crystallised; Diener (1971) discovered viroids. Lichens are symbiotic associations between algae and fungi; the algal component (phycobiont) is autotrophic and the fungal component (mycobiont) is heterotrophic, and they are so closely associated that one would never imagine two organisms within.
Why: The dates give the order Q → S → P → R. Viroids, unlike viruses, lack the protein coat and consist only of free RNA of low molecular weight. Algae prepare food for fungi, and fungi provide shelter and absorb mineral nutrients and water for their partner; lichens are very good pollution indicators because they do not grow in polluted areas.
Why not the others: (A) Order is wrong, and viroids have RNA but no protein coat. (B) Stanley preceded Diener, and Beijerinck preceded both; lichens avoid polluted areas. (C) Order is wrong, and viruses need living host cells.
Key point: 1892 Ivanowsky, 1898 Beijerinck, 1935 Stanley, 1971 Diener (viroid = naked RNA); lichens = pollution indicators.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effects of a microtubule-depolymerising drug on spindles, cilia and cell shape, using the structure of cilia and centrioles
questions.question: A drug that depolymerises microtubules (but does not affect other filaments) is added to a culture of ciliated animal cells. Which set of predicted effects, with its structural reasoning, is correct?
options: A) Only DNA replication stops, because microtubules make DNA
B) The cells keep dividing normally, because spindle fibres are made of actin, and cilia keep beating because their axoneme has no microtubules

C) Dividing cells are arrested because the spindle (formed with the help of centrioles in animal cells) cannot form; cilia stop beating because their core, the axoneme, contains nine pairs of peripheral microtubules and a central pair (9 + 2) that need intact tubulin; and cell shape and support are affected because microtubules are part of the cytoskeleton, the network of filamentous proteins that gives mechanical support, motility and shape; the centriole itself is built of nine peripheral triplets of tubulin in a cartwheel arrangement
D) Ribosomes are destroyed, since they are made of microtubules, so protein synthesis stops at once
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Spindle formation, ciliary beating and cell shape all depend on microtubules.
Concept: An elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures in the cytoplasm is collectively called the cytoskeleton; it is involved in mechanical support, motility and maintenance of the shape of the cell. Cilia and flagella are covered with plasma membrane, and their core, the axoneme, has a number of microtubules running parallel to the long axis: nine doublets of radially arranged peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules (the 9 + 2 array). They emerge from centriole-like structures called basal bodies. Each centriole is made of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein, each a triplet, with a central proteinaceous hub connected to the peripheral tubules by radial spokes (cartwheel organisation). Centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella and the spindle fibres that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.
Why: Every listed function relies on assembled tubulin. Without spindle fibres, chromosomes cannot attach and move, so cells stop at the stage where the spindle should act; without the axoneme's microtubules, cilia cannot bend; without the microtubule part of the cytoskeleton, the cell loses some support and shape.
Why not the others: (A) DNA is made by DNA polymerase, not microtubules. (B) Spindle fibres and the axoneme are microtubule structures. (D) Ribosomes are made of RNA and protein, not microtubules.
Key point: Microtubules build the spindle, the 9 + 2 axoneme and the 9-triplet centriole, and form part of the cytoskeleton.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the structures of starch, cellulose, inulin and chitin and of fatty acids, oils and phospholipids to explain test results and properties
questions.question:
Which set of explanations is correct?
(i) Iodine solution turns a starch suspension blue but gives no blue colour with cotton (cellulose).
(ii) Gingelly (sesame) oil stays liquid in winter, while ghee becomes solid.
(iii) Cell membranes are rich in lecithin.
options: A) (i) Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold I₂ molecules, while cellulose, a polymer of glucose that does not form such complex helices, cannot hold I₂; (ii) oils have lower melting points than fats, so they remain liquid in winter; (iii) lecithin is a phospholipid, a lipid containing phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound, typical of membranes; chitin, the exoskeleton material of arthropods, is a complex polysaccharide containing amino-sugars
B) (i) Cellulose is a protein, so it does not react with iodine; (ii) oils are made of amino acids; (iii) lecithin is a steroid hormone
C) (i) Starch is a polymer of fructose like inulin; (ii) ghee contains no fatty acids; (iii) lecithin is a nucleotide
D) (i) Both starch and cellulose are branched in the same way, so the difference is due to the water; (ii) oils have higher melting points than fats; (iii) membranes have no lipids
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Helical starch traps I₂, cellulose does not; oils have low melting points; lecithin is a membrane phospholipid.
Concept: Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides. Starch is a store house of energy in plant tissues; it forms helical secondary structures and can hold I₂ molecules in the helical portion, giving a blue colour. Cellulose, a polymeric polysaccharide of glucose, does not contain complex helices and hence cannot hold I₂. Inulin is a polymer of fructose. Exoskeletons of arthropods have chitin, a complex polysaccharide with building blocks of amino-sugars and chemically modified sugars. Lipids are generally water-insoluble; a fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group (e.g., palmitic acid has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon). Some lipids have phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound in them; these are phospholipids, found in cell membranes, lecithin being one example.
Why: (i) The test detects the helix, not merely glucose. (ii) Oils have lower melting points (e.g., gingelly oil) and hence remain as oil in winters. (iii) Membranes are built largely of phospholipids such as lecithin.
Why not the others: (B) Cellulose is a polysaccharide, oils are lipids, and lecithin is a phospholipid. (C) Starch is a glucose polymer, ghee is made of fatty-acid esters, and lecithin is not a nucleotide. (D) The two polysaccharides differ in structure, oils have lower melting points, and membranes are lipid-rich.
Key point: Starch helix + I₂ = blue; cellulose no helix; oils melt lower than fats; lecithin = membrane phospholipid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Linking electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity: the chlorine–fluorine anomaly, positive values for noble gases and O⁻, and what electronegativity measures
questions.question: Which set of statements correctly links electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity?
options: A) Fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements because it is the most electronegative; noble gases have large negative electron gain enthalpies
B) Electronegativity is a measurable energy, equal to the electron gain enthalpy expressed in kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is negative
C) Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity both increase down a group because atomic size increases

D) Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, because an electron added to the small, compact 2p subshell of fluorine suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already present, yet fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale); noble gases have positive electron gain enthalpies because the added electron must enter the next higher shell; the second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen (O⁻ → O²⁻) is positive; and electronegativity is not a measurable quantity but describes the ability of a bonded atom to attract shared electrons, rising across a period and falling down a group, opposite to metallic character
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cl has the most negative Δ_egH, F the highest electronegativity; noble gases and O⁻ have positive values; electronegativity is not measurable.
Concept: Electron gain enthalpy (Δ_egH) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom to form an anion; it can be negative (exothermic) or positive. Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself; unlike ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy, it is not a measurable quantity, but scales such as the Pauling scale assign values (F = 4.0).
Why: Generally Δ_egH becomes more negative across a period as effective nuclear charge rises, and less negative down a group as size rises. Fluorine is an exception: its added electron goes into the small n = 2 shell and is repelled strongly, so chlorine's value (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more negative than fluorine's (−328 kJ mol⁻¹). Noble gases have stable configurations, so the incoming electron has to enter a new, higher shell, making the process endothermic. Adding a second electron to O⁻ is opposed by the negative charge already present, so it needs energy. Electronegativity is a property of bonded atoms, and higher electronegativity means more non-metallic character.
Why not the others: (A) Cl, not F, has the most negative Δ_egH, and noble gases have positive values. (B) Electronegativity is not a measurable energy, and O⁻ → O²⁻ is endothermic. (C) Both become less negative/smaller down a group.
Key point: Most negative Δ_egH: Cl; highest electronegativity: F; noble gases and O⁻ → O²⁻ are endothermic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Trends with s-character of sp, sp2 and sp3 carbon, and the shapes and bond lengths that follow from sp3d and sp3d2 hybridisation
questions.question: Which statement about hybridisation trends is correct?
options: A) The s-character of carbon orbitals increases in the order sp < sp² < sp³, so the C–H bond of ethyne is the longest

B) The s-character is 50 % (sp), 33 % (sp²) and 25 % (sp³); as s-character increases, the hybrid orbital is held closer to the nucleus, so the C–H bond becomes shorter and the carbon more electronegative, making the C–H hydrogen of ethyne the most acidic of ethane, ethene and ethyne; in PCl₅ the phosphorus is sp³d hybridised, giving a trigonal bipyramid whose two axial P–Cl bonds are longer than the three equatorial bonds because they suffer more repulsion from the bond pairs, while in SF₆ sulphur is sp³d² hybridised and all six S–F bonds of the octahedron are equal
C) In PCl₅ all five bonds are equal because all five hybrid orbitals are equivalent
D) In SF₆ the sulphur atom uses sp³ hybrid orbitals and two pure d orbitals, so the molecule is a trigonal prism
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Higher s-character gives shorter C–H bonds and more acidic hydrogen; PCl₅ (sp³d) has longer axial bonds; SF₆ (sp³d²) has six equal bonds.
Concept: Hybridisation is the intermixing of orbitals of slightly different energies to give an equal number of new orbitals of equivalent energy and shape. In sp, sp² and sp³ hybrids the s-orbital contributes 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 respectively. Elements of the third period have vacant 3d orbitals of suitable energy, so they can form sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal, as in PCl₅) and sp³d² (octahedral, as in SF₆) hybrids.
Why: An s orbital is more penetrating than a p orbital, so a hybrid with more s-character keeps the bonding electrons nearer the nucleus; the bond is shorter and the carbon effectively more electronegative, which is why the sp carbon of ethyne makes its hydrogen weakly acidic. In PCl₅ the axial bonds make 90° with three equatorial bonds, while each equatorial bond meets only two axial bonds at 90°, so axial bonds are slightly longer and weaker, which also explains why PCl₅ is reactive. All six positions of an octahedron are equivalent.
Why not the others: (A) The order of s-character is reversed, and ethyne's C–H bond is the shortest. (C) Axial and equatorial positions are not equivalent in a trigonal bipyramid. (D) SF₆ uses sp³d² hybrids and is octahedral.
Key point: More s-character → shorter, stronger bond and more electronegative carbon; sp³d = trigonal bipyramid (axial longer); sp³d² = octahedron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining why ionising N2 lengthens its bond but ionising O2 shortens it, using molecular orbital filling, bond order and magnetism
questions.question: Measured bond lengths are: N₂ 110 pm, N₂⁺ 112 pm, O₂ 121 pm and O₂⁺ 112 pm. Removing one electron lengthens the N–N bond but shortens the O–O bond. Which explanation, with the correct magnetic behaviour, is right?
options: A) In N₂ the highest occupied MO is a bonding orbital (σ2p_z), so removing an electron lowers the bond order from 3 to 2.5 and lengthens the bond; in O₂ the highest occupied MOs are the antibonding π*2p orbitals, so removing an electron raises the bond order from 2 to 2.5 and shortens the bond; N₂ is diamagnetic, while N₂⁺, O₂ and O₂⁺ are paramagnetic with 1, 2 and 1 unpaired electrons
B) In both molecules the electron is removed from an antibonding orbital, so both bond orders increase
C) Bond length depends only on the charge, so all cations have shorter bonds than their neutral molecules
D) N₂⁺ has bond order 3.5 and O₂⁺ has bond order 1.5; all four species are diamagnetic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) N₂ loses a bonding electron (bond order 3 → 2.5); O₂ loses an antibonding electron (2 → 2.5).
Concept: Molecular orbital theory fills electrons into bonding and antibonding MOs in order of increasing energy. For molecules up to N₂ the order is σ1s, σ*1s, σ2s, σ*2s, (π2p_x = π2p_y), σ2p_z, (π*2p_x = π*2p_y), σ*2p_z; for O₂ and F₂ the σ2p_z lies below the π2p pair. Bond order = ½(N_b − N_a). A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond. A species with unpaired electrons is paramagnetic.
Why: N₂ (14 electrons): N_b = 10, N_a = 4, bond order 3, all electrons paired; the HOMO σ2p_z is bonding, so N₂⁺ has bond order (9 − 4)/2 = 2.5, a longer bond and one unpaired electron. O₂ (16 electrons): N_b = 10, N_a = 6, bond order 2, with one electron in each π* orbital (paramagnetic, which is why liquid oxygen is attracted by a magnet); removing an antibonding electron gives O₂⁺ with bond order (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5, a shorter bond and one unpaired electron.
Why not the others: (B) The electron from N₂ comes from a bonding MO. (C) The trends are opposite for the two cations, so charge alone cannot decide. (D) Bond orders are 2.5 for both cations, and only N₂ is diamagnetic.
Key point: Removing a bonding electron weakens the bond; removing an antibonding electron strengthens it.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Finding the temperature above which silver oxide decomposes spontaneously from ΔH and ΔS, and the sign of ΔG at room temperature and 600 K
questions.question: Silver oxide is stable at room temperature but gives off oxygen when heated strongly. For Ag₂O(s) → 2Ag(s) + ½O₂(g), ΔH = +31.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +66.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (assume both are constant). Above what temperature is the decomposition spontaneous, and what is ΔG at 298 K and at 600 K?
options: A) Above 2.1 K; ΔG(298 K) = −19.6 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔG(600 K) = −39.6 kJ mol⁻¹
B) It is never spontaneous because ΔH is positive; ΔG is +31.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at all temperatures
C) Above about 470 K; ΔG(298 K) ≈ +11.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (non-spontaneous); ΔG(600 K) ≈ −8.6 kJ mol⁻¹ (spontaneous) — the reaction is driven by entropy at high temperature
D) Below about 470 K; ΔG(298 K) ≈ −11.3 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔG(600 K) ≈ +8.6 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Spontaneous above about 470 K; ΔG = +11.3 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K and −8.6 kJ mol⁻¹ at 600 K.
Concept: The Gibbs energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure: a process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0. When ΔH and ΔS are both positive, the reaction is non-spontaneous at low temperature and becomes spontaneous at high temperature, where the TΔS term outweighs ΔH. The crossover is at T = ΔH/ΔS, where ΔG = 0 and the system is at equilibrium.
Given: ΔH = +31.0 kJ mol⁻¹ = 31 000 J mol⁻¹; ΔS = +66.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; at the crossover, T = ΔH/ΔS.
Step 1: T = 31 000 ÷ 66.0 ≈ 470 K.
Step 2: At 298 K: ΔG = 31.0 − 298 × 0.0660 = 31.0 − 19.7 = +11.3 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: At 600 K: ΔG = 31.0 − 600 × 0.0660 = 31.0 − 39.6 = −8.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: Releasing a gas (½ mol O₂) increases entropy, so ΔS > 0; the decomposition is endothermic. At room temperature the enthalpy term dominates and Ag₂O is stable; above about 470 K (about 197 °C) the entropy term dominates and the oxide decomposes.
Why not the others: (A) Uses ΔH in kJ with ΔS in J (unit slip) and drops ΔH from ΔG. (B) A positive ΔH does not forbid spontaneity when ΔS > 0. (D) The signs are reversed: with both ΔH and ΔS positive, high temperature favours the reaction.
Key point: ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0 → spontaneous only above T = ΔH/ΔS.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading a pressure–volume table for a fixed mass of nitrogen to confirm Boyle's law, find the amount of gas, its density, and the volume after heating at constant pressure
questions.question:
A fixed mass of nitrogen (M = 28 g mol⁻¹) at 300 K gives these readings:
P (bar) | 1.00 | 2.00 | 4.00
V (L) | 24.9 | 12.45 | 6.23
The gas at 2.00 bar is then heated to 450 K at constant pressure. Using R = 0.083 bar L K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what are the amount of gas, its density at 1.00 bar and 300 K, and its new volume at 450 K?
options: B) 1.00 mol; 0.89 g L⁻¹; 12.45 L, because volume does not depend on temperature at constant pressure
C) 1.00 mol; 1.12 g L⁻¹; 18.7 L — the product PV is constant (24.9 bar L) at fixed temperature (Boyle's law), and at constant pressure V is proportional to the absolute temperature (Charles's law)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) n = 1.00 mol; density 1.12 g L⁻¹; V = 18.7 L at 450 K.
Concept: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas varies inversely with its volume (PV = constant). Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. Combining these with Avogadro's law gives the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Density of a gas d = PM/RT.
Given: PV readings at 300 K; M = 28 g mol⁻¹; R = 0.083 bar L K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; heated to 450 K at 2.00 bar.
Formula/Principle: PV = nRT; d = m/V = nM/V; V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ at constant P.
Step 1: PV = 1.00 × 24.9 = 2.00 × 12.45 = 4.00 × 6.23 ≈ 24.9 bar L, constant, so Boyle's law holds.
Step 2: n = PV/RT = 24.9 ÷ (0.083 × 300) = 24.9 ÷ 24.9 = 1.00 mol.
Step 3: Density at 1.00 bar = (1.00 × 28) g ÷ 24.9 L = 1.12 g L⁻¹.
Step 4: V₂ = 12.45 × 450/300 = 18.7 L (check: nRT/P = 0.083 × 450 ÷ 2.00 = 18.7 L).
Why: The constant product PV at one temperature identifies Boyle behaviour; the ideal gas equation then fixes n, and heating at constant pressure scales the volume by T₂/T₁ (on the kelvin scale).
Why not the others: (A) Doubles n, which would double PV. (B) Ignores Charles's law, and the density uses the wrong volume. (D) Halves n and uses the wrong temperature ratio.
Key point: PV constant at fixed T; V ∝ T at fixed P; n = PV/RT.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why Ag2CrO4 is more soluble than AgCl although its Ksp is much smaller, and the ionic-product condition for precipitation
questions.question: At 298 K, K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and K_sp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which comparison of their molar solubilities in water is correct, and when will a precipitate form on mixing solutions?
options: A) s(AgCl) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M and s(Ag₂CrO₄) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M, so Ag₂CrO₄ is about five times more soluble even though its K_sp is smaller, because K_sp values can be compared directly only for salts of the same formula type; a precipitate forms when the ionic product (Q_sp, calculated with the actual ion concentrations raised to their stoichiometric powers) exceeds K_sp
B) AgCl is more soluble because its K_sp is larger; a precipitate forms whenever two solutions containing the ions are mixed
C) s(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M and s(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹² M; a precipitate forms only when Q_sp is less than K_sp
D) Both have the same solubility, because both contain silver ions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) s(AgCl) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M, s(Ag₂CrO₄) ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M; precipitation occurs when Q_sp > K_sp.
Concept: For a sparingly soluble salt MₓXᵧ in equilibrium with its saturated solution, K_sp = [M^{y+}]ˣ[X^{x−}]ʸ, the solubility product constant. If the molar solubility is s, then K_sp = (xs)ˣ(ys)ʸ = xˣyʸ s^{x+y}. Whenever the ionic product of a solution exceeds K_sp, the excess ions combine and precipitate until the product falls to K_sp.
Given: K_sp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰; K_sp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
Formula/Principle: AgCl: K_sp = s²; Ag₂CrO₄: K_sp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³.
Step 1: s(AgCl) = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 2: s(Ag₂CrO₄) = (1.1 × 10⁻¹² ÷ 4)^{1/3} = (2.75 × 10⁻¹³)^{1/3} ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 3: Ratio ≈ 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 4.9.
Why: Because K_sp of Ag₂CrO₄ involves s³ (with a factor 4) while that of AgCl involves s², a smaller K_sp can still correspond to a larger solubility. Only salts with the same ion ratio (e.g., AgCl and AgBr) can be ranked by K_sp alone.
Why not the others: (B) Ranking by K_sp fails for different formula types, and mixing gives a precipitate only if Q_sp > K_sp. (C) Confuses K_sp with solubility and reverses the precipitation condition. (D) Solubility depends on the whole equilibrium, not on a shared ion.
Key point: Compare solubilities, not K_sp, for salts of different types; precipitate when Q_sp > K_sp.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Ranking groups by inductive effect, its fall-off along a chain, carbocation stability from alkyl +I effects, and the temporary nature of the electromeric effect
questions.question: Which set of statements about inductive and electromeric effects is correct?
options: A) The −I effect increases in the order NO₂ < CN < F < Cl; the inductive effect grows stronger with every additional bond from the substituent
B) The electromeric effect is a permanent polarisation present even in the absence of any reagent, like the inductive effect
C) Alkyl groups withdraw electrons (−I), so a methyl carbocation is more stable than a tertiary carbocation

D) Among common groups, the electron-withdrawing (−I) order is NO₂ > CN > COOH > F > Cl > Br > I > OH > OR > C₆H₅; the inductive effect, a permanent polarisation transmitted through σ bonds, decreases rapidly with distance and is negligible beyond about three bonds; alkyl groups are electron-releasing (+I), so the stability of carbocations increases methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary; and the electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of a shared π-electron pair to one atom of a multiple bond, occurring only in the presence of an attacking reagent and vanishing when it is removed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The −I order, the fall-off with distance, the +I stabilisation of carbocations and the temporary electromeric effect are all stated correctly.
Concept: When a covalent bond is formed between atoms of different electronegativity, the electron density shifts towards the more electronegative atom, and this polarisation is transmitted along a chain of σ bonds: the inductive effect. Groups that withdraw electron density show a −I effect, and groups that release it (such as alkyl groups) show a +I effect. The electromeric (E) effect is a temporary effect, operating in compounds with a multiple bond when attacked by a reagent: if the π electrons move towards the atom to which the reagent attaches, it is +E; if away, −E.
Why: The −I sequence reflects the electron-pulling power of each group. Each successive σ bond passes on only part of the polarisation, so the effect dies out within about three bonds. Alkyl groups push electron density towards a positive centre, dispersing its charge; more alkyl groups mean greater stability (tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl). The electromeric effect is a response to the reagent's demand for electrons; when both inductive and electromeric effects act in opposite directions, the electromeric effect predominates.
Why not the others: (A) The order is reversed, and the effect weakens with distance. (B) The electromeric effect is temporary and needs a reagent. (C) Alkyl groups are +I, so tertiary carbocations are the most stable.
Key point: −I: NO₂ > CN > COOH > F > Cl…; inductive effect fades within about three bonds; +I alkyls stabilise carbocations; E effect is temporary.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking phenol, toluene, benzene, chlorobenzene and nitrobenzene by rate of electrophilic substitution and naming the positions attacked
questions.question: Phenol, toluene, benzene, chlorobenzene and nitrobenzene are nitrated separately under comparable conditions. Which statement about their relative rates and the main positions substituted is correct?
options: A) Nitrobenzene > chlorobenzene > benzene > toluene > phenol; all five are substituted mainly at the meta position

B) Phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene; phenol and toluene are activated and give mainly ortho and para products, chlorobenzene is deactivated but still ortho/para directing (its −I effect outweighs its +R effect in rate, while the +R effect decides the positions), and nitrobenzene is strongly deactivated and gives mainly the meta product
C) Toluene > phenol > nitrobenzene > benzene > chlorobenzene; nitrobenzene gives mainly ortho and para products
D) All five react at the same rate, because the electrophile is the same nitronium ion; only the positions differ
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene; OH, CH₃ and Cl direct ortho/para, NO₂ directs meta.
Concept: When monosubstituted benzene undergoes further substitution, the existing group affects both the ease of reaction and the position of the incoming group (directive influence). Activating groups such as –OH and –CH₃ donate electrons to the ring, increasing electron density, especially at ortho and para positions, and so direct the electrophile there. Deactivating groups such as –NO₂ withdraw electrons, reducing electron density, especially at ortho and para positions, so the meta position is comparatively richer and is attacked. Halogens are an exception: they are deactivating because of their strong −I effect but ortho/para directing because of resonance (+R).
Why: –OH donates strongly by resonance, so phenol reacts fastest; –CH₃ donates by inductive effect and hyperconjugation, so toluene is faster than benzene. Chlorine withdraws inductively more than it donates by resonance, so chlorobenzene is slower than benzene, but the resonance structures still place negative charge at ortho and para positions. –NO₂ withdraws by both −I and −R, so nitrobenzene is slowest and gives m-dinitrobenzene.
Why not the others: (A) The rate order is reversed, and only NO₂ directs meta. (C) Phenol is faster than toluene, and nitrobenzene is the slowest and meta-directing. (D) The substituent changes the electron density of the ring, so rates differ greatly.
Key point: Activators (OH > CH₃): faster, o/p; halogens: slower, o/p; NO₂: slowest, meta.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing staggered and eclipsed ethane, the steps of free-radical chlorination of methane, why traces of ethane form, and the reactivity trend of halogens
questions.question: Which statement about the conformations of ethane and the free-radical halogenation of alkanes is correct?
options: A) The eclipsed conformation of ethane is more stable than the staggered one, and the two can be separated at room temperature

B) The staggered conformation of ethane is more stable than the eclipsed one by only about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ (torsional strain), so rotation about the C–C bond is almost free at room temperature and the conformers cannot be separated; chlorination of methane in light proceeds by initiation (homolysis of Cl₂), propagation (Cl• abstracts H to give CH₃•, which reacts with Cl₂) and termination, and a little ethane forms when two CH₃• radicals combine in a termination step; the reactivity of halogens is F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂, and iodination is reversible, so it needs an oxidising agent such as HIO₃ or HNO₃
C) The chlorination of methane starts by heterolysis of Cl₂ into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻, and ethane forms by an ionic rearrangement
D) Iodine reacts with alkanes faster than fluorine, because iodine is the largest halogen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Staggered is more stable by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹; chlorination is a radical chain; ethane comes from CH₃• + CH₃•; reactivity F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
Concept: Rotation about a C–C single bond gives an infinite number of spatial arrangements called conformations. In ethane, the staggered form has the hydrogens of the two carbons as far apart as possible, while in the eclipsed form they are closest; the repulsion between bond clouds in the eclipsed form is torsional strain. Halogenation of alkanes in diffused sunlight, UV light or at high temperature proceeds by a free radical chain mechanism with three steps: initiation, propagation and termination.
Why: The energy difference of about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ is so small that at ordinary temperatures thermal energy lets molecules interconvert, so it is not possible to separate the conformers. In chlorination, initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•; propagation: CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl, then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; termination: two radicals combine, e.g., Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl, CH₃• + CH₃• → CH₃–CH₃, which explains traces of ethane. Fluorination is too violent to control, and iodination is very slow and reversible, because the HI formed reduces the alkyl iodide back unless it is oxidised.
Why not the others: (A) Staggered is more stable, and the conformers interconvert too fast to separate. (C) The reaction begins with homolytic fission, and ethane forms by radical combination. (D) Reactivity decreases from fluorine to iodine.
Key point: Staggered ethane is favoured by about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹; halogenation is a radical chain (initiation, propagation, termination); F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using Raoult's law with measured vapour pressure to detect positive deviation, its thermodynamic signs and the vapour composition of an ideal mixture
questions.question: At a given temperature, pure liquids A and B have vapour pressures of 450 mm Hg and 700 mm Hg. A mixture with x_A = 0.40 is found to have a total vapour pressure of 690 mm Hg. What total vapour pressure does Raoult's law predict, what does the measured value show, and what would the mole fraction of B in the vapour be if the mixture were ideal?
options: A) 575 mm Hg; negative deviation; ΔmixH < 0; y_B = 0.40
