Answer: (A) 2.2 s, 2.0 s, \(\sqrt3\approx1.73\) s, \(2\sqrt6\approx4.9\) s.
Given: \(T_0=2.0\ \text{s}=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}};\ \text{lift accelerating up: }g_{\text{eff}}=g+a\)
Step 1: \(\text{(i) }L\to1.21L:\ T=2.0\sqrt{1.21}=2.0\times1.1=2.2\ \text{s}\)
Step 2: \(\text{(ii) mass does not appear: }T=2.0\ \text{s}\)
Step 3: \(\text{(iii) }g_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac43g:\ T=2.0\sqrt{\tfrac34}=\sqrt3\approx1.73\ \text{s}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{(iv) }g_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac g6:\ T=2.0\sqrt6\approx4.90\ \text{s}\]
Check: \[T\propto\sqrt{L}\text{ and }T\propto\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{g_{\text{eff}}}}\text{: longer string or weaker gravity → slower swings}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the restoring force and the inertia are both proportional to the bob's mass, so mass cancels; only }L\text{ and the effective gravity matter}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }T\propto L\text{ and }T\propto m\); (C) \(\text{uses }T\propto1/\sqrt m\text{ and inverts the lift and Moon effects}\); (D) \(\text{uses }g-a\text{ for an upward acceleration}\).
Key point: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g_{\text{eff}}}\text{, independent of mass}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How the fields of a point charge, an infinite line charge and an infinite plane sheet scale when the distance is doubled
questions.question: At distance \(r\), a point charge, a long straight uniformly charged wire and a large uniformly charged plane sheet each produce an electric field of magnitude \(E_0\). What field does each produce at distance \(2r\)?
options: B) \(E_0/4\), \(E_0/2\), \(E_0\): the point-charge field falls as \(1/r^2\), the line-charge field as \(1/r\), and the sheet field \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) does not depend on distance
C) \(E_0/4\) for all three, because all fields obey the inverse-square law
D) \(E_0/2\) for all three, because the charge is the same
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(E_0/4\), \(E_0/2\), \(E_0\).
Given: \(\text{each field}=E_0\text{ at }r;\ \text{new distance }2r\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_{\text{point}}=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2};\ E_{\text{line}}=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r};\ E_{\text{sheet}}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(E_{\text{point}}\propto r^{-2}\Rightarrow E=\tfrac{E_0}{4}\)
Step 2: \(E_{\text{line}}\propto r^{-1}\Rightarrow E=\tfrac{E_0}{2}\)
Step 3: \(E_{\text{sheet}}\propto r^{0}\Rightarrow E=E_0\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Gauss: }E\cdot4\pi r^2=\tfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0};\ E\cdot2\pi rl=\tfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0};\ E\cdot2A=\tfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[\text{field lines spread over a sphere }(\propto r^2)\text{, a cylinder }(\propto r)\text{ or not at all (parallel lines from a plane)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area over which the flux spreads grows as }r^2,\ r\text{ and }r^0\text{ for the three symmetries}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{wrong powers}\); (C) \(\text{only the point charge follows the inverse square}\); (D) \(\text{distance dependence differs by geometry}\).
Key point: \(\text{point }1/r^2,\ \text{line }1/r,\ \text{sheet constant}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using mapped equipotential lines to find the field strength and direction, and the path-independent work done in moving a charge between them
questions.question: In an experiment on a conducting sheet, equipotential lines of 8 V, 6 V, 4 V and 2 V are found to be straight, parallel and 2.0 cm apart. What is the electric field, how much work does the field do when a +3.0 µC charge moves from the 8 V line to the 2 V line, and how much when it moves along the 6 V line?
options: A) 400 V m⁻¹ parallel to the lines; \(-1.8\times10^{-5}\) J; \(1.8\times10^{-5}\) J
B) 100 V m⁻¹ from the 2 V line towards the 8 V line; \(6\times10^{-6}\) J; zero
C) 1.0 V m⁻¹ perpendicular to the lines; \(1.8\times10^{-5}\) J only along a straight path; zero
D) 100 V m⁻¹, perpendicular to the lines and pointing from 8 V towards 2 V; \(+1.8\times10^{-5}\) J by the field (the potential energy falls by this amount) along any path; zero along the 6 V line
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(E=100\ \text{V m}^{-1}\) from high to low potential; \(W=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{J}\) on any path; zero along an equipotential.
Given: \(\Delta V=2\ \text{V per }0.020\ \text{m};\ q=3.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{C};\ V_A=8\ \text{V},\ V_B=2\ \text{V}\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr}\Rightarrow|E|=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta r};\ W_{\text{field}}=q(V_A-V_B)\)
Step 1: \(|E|=\dfrac{2}{0.020}=100\ \text{V m}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\text{direction: perpendicular to equipotentials, towards decreasing }V\ (8\ \text{V}\to2\ \text{V})\)
Step 3: \(W_{\text{field}}=3.0\times10^{-6}\times(8-2)=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=-W_{\text{field}}=-1.8\times10^{-5}\ \text{J};\ \text{along the 6 V line }\Delta V=0\Rightarrow W=0\]
Check: \[E\times d=100\times0.060=6\ \text{V}=8-2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the electrostatic force is conservative, so work depends only on the end potentials; no work is done along an equipotential because the field is perpendicular to it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{field is perpendicular to equipotentials, and sign errors}\); (B) \(\text{direction reversed and }\Delta V\text{ taken as 2 V}\); (C) \(\text{unit slip (cm) and wrongly path-dependent}\).
Key point: \(E=\Delta V/\Delta r\perp\text{equipotentials, from high to low }V;\ W=q\Delta V\text{ (path-independent)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading a galvanometer-current versus applied-voltage line to find the series resistance of a voltmeter, and the shunt for an ammeter
questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 2.0 mA. After it is converted into a voltmeter, a graph of galvanometer current against applied voltage is a straight line through the origin reaching 2.0 mA at 10 V. What series resistance was used, and what shunt would convert the same galvanometer into an ammeter of range 0–1.0 A?
options: A) 5000 Ω in parallel; 50 Ω in series
B) 4950 Ω in parallel; 0.10 Ω in series
C) 5050 Ω in series; 10 Ω shunt
D) 4950 Ω in series (total 5000 Ω, the reciprocal of the slope \(2.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{A V}^{-1}\)); a shunt of about 0.10 Ω in parallel
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Series 4950 Ω; shunt ≈ 0.10 Ω.
Given: \(G=50\ \Omega,\ I_g=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{A};\ \text{slope}=\tfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{10}=2.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{A V}^{-1};\ I=1.0\ \text{A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{voltmeter: }I_g=\dfrac{V}{G+R};\ \text{ammeter: }I_gG=(I-I_g)S\)
Step 1: \(G+R=\dfrac{1}{\text{slope}}=\dfrac{10}{2.0\times10^{-3}}=5000\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(R=5000-50=4950\ \Omega\text{ (in series)}\)
Step 3: \(S=\dfrac{I_gG}{I-I_g}=\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}\times50}{0.998}\)
Worked derivation: \[S=\dfrac{0.10}{0.998}\approx0.1002\ \Omega\approx0.10\ \Omega\text{ (in parallel)}\]
Check: \[\text{voltmeter resistance }5000\ \Omega\gg\text{ammeter resistance }\approx0.10\ \Omega\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a high series resistance limits the current for a given voltage (voltmeter); a low shunt carries most of the current around the galvanometer (ammeter)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{connections swapped}\); (B) \(\text{connections swapped}\); (C) \(\text{adds }G\text{ instead of subtracting, and the shunt is far too large}\).
Key point: \(R=\tfrac{V}{I_g}-G\text{ in series};\ S=\tfrac{I_gG}{I-I_g}\text{ in parallel}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Motional emf across the wings of an aircraft in the Earth's vertical field and across a rod rotating about one end
questions.question: (i) An aircraft of wing span 30 m flies horizontally at 250 m s⁻¹ where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is \(4.0\times10^{-5}\) T. (ii) A metal rod of length 0.50 m rotates at 120 rad s⁻¹ about one end, in a plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.40 T. What emf is induced in each case?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.30 V and 6.0 V.
Given: \(\text{(i) }l=30\ \text{m},\ v=250\ \text{m s}^{-1},\ B_V=4.0\times10^{-5}\ \text{T};\ \text{(ii) }l=0.50\ \text{m},\ \omega=120\ \text{rad s}^{-1},\ B=0.40\ \text{T}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=Blv;\ \text{rotating rod: }\varepsilon=\int_0^l B\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega l^2\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon_1=4.0\times10^{-5}\times30\times250\)
Step 2: \(\varepsilon_1=0.30\ \text{V}\)
Step 3: \(\varepsilon_2=\tfrac12\times0.40\times120\times(0.50)^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\varepsilon_2=0.5\times0.40\times120\times0.25=6.0\ \text{V}\]
Check: \[\text{rod: average speed of the rod}=\tfrac12\omega l=30\ \text{m s}^{-1};\ \varepsilon=Bl\bar v=0.40\times0.50\times30=6.0\ \text{V}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only the field component perpendicular to both the conductor and its velocity matters: for a horizontal wing moving horizontally, that is the vertical component; along a rotating rod, the speed grows linearly from the pivot}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{power-of-ten slip and drops the }\tfrac12\); (B) \(\text{factor-of-10 slip and uses }B\omega l^2\); (D) \(\text{drops the }\tfrac12\text{ for the rotating rod}\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon=Blv\text{ for translation};\ \varepsilon=\tfrac12B\omega l^2\text{ for rotation about one end}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Scaling of generator emf with rotation speed, and how stepping up the transmission voltage tenfold reduces line current and I²R loss
questions.question: (i) An AC generator's coil is made to rotate twice as fast. (ii) A power station sends 100 kW through lines of total resistance 4.0 Ω, first at 2.0 kV and then, using an ideal step-up transformer, at 20 kV. What happens to the generator's peak emf and frequency, and what are the line losses in the two cases?
options: A) Peak emf and frequency both double (\(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega\)); line current falls from 50 A to 5.0 A, so the loss falls from 10 kW to 100 W, a factor of 100
B) Peak emf doubles but frequency is unchanged; losses fall from 10 kW to 1 kW
C) Peak emf is unchanged but frequency doubles; losses are the same because the power is the same
D) Peak emf quadruples; losses rise from 100 W to 10 kW because the voltage is higher
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Peak emf and frequency double; losses 10 kW → 100 W.
Given: \(\omega\to2\omega;\ P=1.0\times10^5\ \text{W},\ R=4.0\ \Omega,\ V_1=2.0\times10^3\ \text{V},\ V_2=2.0\times10^4\ \text{V}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t\Rightarrow\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega,\ \nu=\tfrac{\omega}{2\pi};\ I=\tfrac PV;\ P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R\)
Step 1: \(\omega\to2\omega\Rightarrow\varepsilon_0\to2\varepsilon_0,\ \nu\to2\nu\)
Step 2: \(I_1=\dfrac{10^5}{2000}=50\ \text{A};\ P_1=50^2\times4.0=10\,000\ \text{W}\)
Step 3: \(I_2=\dfrac{10^5}{20\,000}=5.0\ \text{A};\ P_2=25\times4.0=100\ \text{W}\)
Worked derivation: \[\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}=\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^2=100\]
Check: \[\text{ideal transformer: }V_pI_p=V_sI_s\Rightarrow\text{10 times the voltage means }\tfrac1{10}\text{ the current}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{faster rotation changes the flux faster (larger emf) and completes more cycles per second; for fixed power, a higher voltage needs a smaller current, and the loss depends on }I^2\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{frequency doubles, and the loss scales as }I^2\); (C) \(\varepsilon_0\propto\omega\text{, and the loss depends on current}\); (D) \(\varepsilon_0\propto\omega\text{, not }\omega^2\text{, and losses fall}\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega;\ P_{\text{loss}}=(P/V)^2R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Radius of the bright circle through which light from a submerged point source escapes, using the critical angle for water
questions.question: A small bulb is placed 2.0 m below the surface of a still pond (refractive index of water \(\tfrac43\)). Light leaves the surface only through a circular patch directly above the bulb. What is the critical angle, the radius of the patch, and what happens to rays striking the surface outside it?
options: A) \(\sin C=\tfrac43\); 2.0 m; they refract into air at grazing angles

B) \(\sin C=\tfrac34\) (\(C\approx48.6^\circ\)); radius \(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{n^2-1}}=\dfrac{6}{\sqrt7}\approx2.3\) m; rays outside the patch meet the surface at more than the critical angle and are totally internally reflected back into the water
C) \(\sin C=\tfrac34\); 1.5 m; they are absorbed by the surface
D) \(\sin C=\tfrac12\); 3.5 m; they pass straight through
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\sin C=\tfrac34\); \(r=\tfrac{6}{\sqrt7}\approx2.27\ \text{m}\); outside rays undergo total internal reflection.
Given: \(n=\tfrac43,\ h=2.0\ \text{m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin C=\tfrac1n;\ r=h\tan C\)
Step 1: \(\sin C=\tfrac34\Rightarrow C\approx48.6^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\cos C=\sqrt{1-\tfrac9{16}}=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{4}\Rightarrow\tan C=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt7}\)
Step 3: \(r=2.0\times\tfrac{3}{\sqrt7}=\tfrac{6}{\sqrt7}\)
Worked derivation: \[r=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{n^2-1}}=\dfrac{2.0}{\sqrt{16/9-1}}=\dfrac{2.0}{\sqrt7/3}\approx2.27\ \text{m}\]
Check: \[\text{at the rim, angle of incidence }=C\Rightarrow\text{refracted ray grazes the surface }(n\sin C=1)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{going from denser to rarer medium, rays incident beyond the critical angle cannot refract out; the boundary of the escape cone is set by }C\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\sin C\text{ cannot exceed 1}\); (C) \(\text{uses }r=h\sin C\text{-type slip, and the light is reflected, not absorbed}\); (D) \(\text{wrong critical angle}\).
Key point: \(\sin C=1/n;\ \text{escape-circle radius }h/\sqrt{n^2-1}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the intensity pattern from two slits lit by one laser (coherent) with that from two independent lamps (incoherent)
questions.question: Two identical narrow slits, each giving intensity \(I_0\) on a screen alone, are lit (a) by a single laser beam that covers both slits, and (b) by two separate identical lamps, one behind each slit. Which comparison is correct?
options: A) Both give bright and dark fringes, with maxima of \(4I_0\)

B) (a) gives a stable fringe pattern with \(I=4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)\), so maxima are \(4I_0\) and minima zero; (b) gives a uniform intensity \(2I_0\), because the phase difference between independent sources changes rapidly and randomly and the \(\cos\phi\) term averages to zero; the average intensity is \(2I_0\) in both cases, so energy is only redistributed in (a)
C) (a) gives a uniform intensity \(4I_0\) everywhere; (b) gives fringes
D) Neither gives fringes, because the two slits are separate sources
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Coherent: fringes between \(4I_0\) and 0; incoherent: uniform \(2I_0\); average \(2I_0\) in both.
Given: \(I_1=I_2=I_0;\ \text{phase difference }\phi\text{ at a point}\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(\text{(a) }\phi\text{ fixed at each point: }I=2I_0(1+\cos\phi)=4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)\)
Step 2: \(I_{\max}=4I_0\ (\phi=2n\pi),\ I_{\min}=0\ (\phi=(2n+1)\pi)\)
Step 3: \(\text{(b) }\phi\text{ varies randomly in time: }\langle\cos\phi\rangle=0\Rightarrow I=2I_0\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{average over a fringe in (a): }\langle4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)\rangle=4I_0\times\tfrac12=2I_0\]
Check: \[\text{total energy is the same in (a) and (b); interference only redistributes it}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{interference needs a constant phase difference; one laser feeding both slits supplies it, while two independent lamps emit with phases that change in a random way}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{incoherent sources give no stable fringes}\); (C) \(\text{the cases are reversed}\); (D) \(\text{slits lit by one coherent source behave as coherent sources}\).
Key point: \(\text{coherent: }I=4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2);\ \text{incoherent: }I=2I_0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Comparing maximum kinetic energy, stopping potential and photocurrent for photons of different energy and for a change of intensity
questions.question: A metal has work function 2.0 eV. It is lit in turn by (a) photons of energy 3.0 eV, (b) photons of energy 4.0 eV, (c) the 3.0 eV light at double the intensity, and (d) very intense light of photon energy 1.8 eV. Which comparison is correct? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
options: A) \(K_{\max}\) is 1.5 eV in (a) and 3.0 eV in (b); (c) doubles \(K_{\max}\); (d) emits slowly after a delay
B) Stopping potentials are 3.0 V and 4.0 V; (c) halves the stopping potential; (d) emits a few electrons
C) \(K_{\max}\) is the same in (a) and (b), because the metal is the same; (d) emits because the intensity is high

D) \(K_{\max}=1.0\) eV in (a) and 2.0 eV in (b), with stopping potentials 1.0 V and 2.0 V; (c) doubles the saturation photocurrent but leaves \(K_{\max}\) and the stopping potential unchanged; (d) gives no emission at all, since 1.8 eV is below the work function (threshold wavelength 620 nm)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(K_{\max}\) 1.0 and 2.0 eV; intensity changes only the current; no emission below threshold.
Given: \(\phi_0=2.0\ \text{eV};\ h\nu=3.0,\ 4.0,\ 1.8\ \text{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(K_{\max}=h\nu-\phi_0=eV_0;\ \lambda_0=\tfrac{hc}{\phi_0}\)
Step 1: \(\text{(a) }K_{\max}=3.0-2.0=1.0\ \text{eV}\Rightarrow V_0=1.0\ \text{V}\)
Step 2: \(\text{(b) }K_{\max}=4.0-2.0=2.0\ \text{eV}\Rightarrow V_0=2.0\ \text{V}\)
Step 3: \(\text{(c) twice the photons per second}\Rightarrow\text{twice the saturation current; }K_{\max}=1.0\ \text{eV}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{(d) }h\nu=1.8<2.0\ \text{eV}\Rightarrow\text{no emission};\ \lambda_0=\tfrac{1240}{2.0}=620\ \text{nm}\]
Check: \[V_0\text{ against }\nu\text{ is a straight line of slope }h/e\text{; doubling intensity does not move it}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each electron absorbs one photon; the photon energy sets the maximum kinetic energy, and intensity sets only how many photons arrive per second; emission is instantaneous above threshold}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{wrong subtraction; intensity does not raise }K_{\max}\text{, and there is no delay}\); (B) \(\text{forgets the work function}\); (C) \(K_{\max}\text{ depends on frequency; below threshold intensity cannot cause emission}\).
Key point: \(eV_0=h\nu-\phi_0;\ \text{intensity}\to\text{current only}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Formation of the depletion layer and barrier potential, and how forward and reverse bias change the barrier and the current
questions.question: Which description of a p-n junction diode is correct?
options: A) When the junction forms, holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p, leaving immobile ions near the junction that form a depletion layer and set up a barrier potential opposing further diffusion; forward bias lowers the barrier and narrows the depletion layer, so a large current of majority carriers flows, while reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the layer, leaving only a small current of minority carriers that is nearly independent of voltage until breakdown
B) The depletion layer contains a large number of free electrons and holes, which carry the current in reverse bias
C) Forward bias widens the depletion layer, and the current falls as the voltage increases
D) The reverse current is carried by majority carriers and increases in proportion to the reverse voltage
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Diffusion builds a depletion layer and barrier; forward bias lowers it (large majority current), reverse bias raises it (small minority current).
Given: \(\text{p-type: majority holes};\ \text{n-type: majority electrons}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{diffusion current (majority) vs drift current (minority); equilibrium when they balance}\)
Step 1: \(\text{diffusion leaves uncovered acceptor ions }(-)\text{ on the p side and donor ions }(+)\text{ on the n side}\)
Step 2: \(\text{the field from n to p sets up a barrier potential }V_0\text{ that opposes further diffusion}\)
Step 3: \(\text{forward bias }V:\ \text{barrier}\to V_0-V\text{, layer narrows};\ \text{reverse bias: barrier}\to V_0+V\text{, layer widens}\)
Worked derivation: \[I_{\text{forward}}\text{ rises steeply once }V\text{ exceeds the threshold (about 0.7 V for Si)};\ I_{\text{reverse}}\sim\mu\text{A, until breakdown}\]
Check: \[\text{reverse current depends on the number of minority carriers (temperature), not on voltage}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the depletion layer has no mobile charges; lowering the barrier lets majority carriers cross freely, while raising it lets only the few minority carriers drift across}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the depletion layer is depleted of mobile carriers}\); (C) \(\text{forward bias narrows the layer and the current rises}\); (D) \(\text{reverse current is due to minority carriers and is almost constant}\).
Key point: \(\text{forward: lower barrier, large majority current; reverse: higher barrier, tiny minority current}\)

questions.sub_topic: Converting the gravitational constant from SI to CGS units by scaling each base unit, and the size of the erg
questions.question: The gravitational constant is \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{kg}^{-2}\). What is its value in CGS units (dyn cm² g⁻²), and how many ergs make one joule?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(6.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{dyn cm}^2\,\text{g}^{-2}\); \(1\ \text{J}=10^7\ \text{erg}\).
Given: \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{kg}^{-2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(1\ \text{N}=10^5\ \text{dyn},\ 1\ \text{m}=10^2\ \text{cm},\ 1\ \text{kg}=10^3\ \text{g};\ [G]=\text{M}^{-1}\text{L}^3\text{T}^{-2}\)
Step 1: \(1\ \text{m}^2=10^4\ \text{cm}^2;\ 1\ \text{kg}^{-2}=10^{-6}\ \text{g}^{-2}\)
Step 2: \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\times10^5\times10^4\times10^{-6}\)
Step 3: \(G=6.67\times10^{-11+3}=6.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{dyn cm}^2\,\text{g}^{-2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{dimensional check: }n_2=n_1\left(\tfrac{M_1}{M_2}\right)^{-1}\left(\tfrac{L_1}{L_2}\right)^{3}\left(\tfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^{-2}=6.67\times10^{-11}\times(10^3)^{-1}\times(10^2)^3=6.67\times10^{-8}\]
Check: \[1\ \text{J}=1\ \text{N}\times1\ \text{m}=10^5\ \text{dyn}\times10^2\ \text{cm}=10^7\ \text{erg}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a physical quantity is the same in any system; its numerical value scales inversely with the size of the unit}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses the wrong exponent for length, and inverts the erg}\); (B) \(\text{no conversion}\); (D) \(\text{wrong power of length and energy}\).
Key point: \(n_1u_1=n_2u_2;\ \text{convert each base unit with its dimensional power}\)
